articles.title: Sweden’s Far Right: Faltering but Not Defeated
articles.author: Nicola Quondamatteo
articles.content: For the far-right Sweden Democrats, Sunday’s parliamentary elections may have looked like the final step toward full “detoxification.” Success in the election for the Riksdag promised to crown the party’s integration into the Swedish political system — a formality by this point, but a significant step nonetheless. That integration had substantially taken place already four years ago, when a government coalition deal was agreed on at the Tidö Castle. The Sweden Democrats had previously been subject to a cordon sanitaire excluding them from office: the Moderate Party leader, Ulf Kristersson, even solemnly promised a Holocaust survivor that he would never cooperate with the far right. But after the 2022 elections, this pledge was ditched. Kristersson soon formed a coalition of traditional center-right parties (Moderates, Christian Democrats, and Liberals), which relied on the outside support of the Sweden Democrats, who had placed second in that vote. The establishment was betting on moderating the far-right party. In reality, the opposite happened: the Sweden Democrats reaped the benefits of normalization, and the traditional right shifted to a harder line on immigration and criminal justice policy while also dismantling climate policies. This is no national peculiarity. Through European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s second term, we have seen a similar process in the EU institutions themselves, with a slew of deregulation, the shelving of the Green Deal, and a migration policy coordinated between Christian democracy and the various forces of the far-right front. The Sweden Democrats’ leader, Jimmie Åkesson, had his sights on breaking the last taboo: a full and direct entry of his party into government, taking over key ministries. The traditional right-wing parties had accepted this, albeit with some internal unease in the Liberals’ case. Already, over the past four years, the boundaries of what is possible in Sweden have been pushed far beyond previous limits. Take the cases of the young adults with an immigrant background being deported to their parents’ countries of origin (including to such unsafe countries as Egypt or even Iran), while their families remain in Sweden. From this perspective, the alarms raised by Human Rights Watch come as no surprise; Greta Thunberg denounced her own country’s government. The Sweden Democrats’ election campaign raised the stakes. One Riksdag member, Richard Jomshof, openly described himself as Islamophobic. To those who pointed out that not all Muslims fit his racist stereotype, he replied contemptuously: “Then they can stop being Muslims.” In western Sweden, the party went so far as to plaster public transit buses with advertisements reading: “Do you miss Mogadishu? Remigration will help you go home,” sparking protests from some drivers of Somali origin. Ultimately, the election saw Åkesson’s bid for ministerial power repelled — albeit by a narrow margin, and with a smaller gap than indicated by recent opinion polling and even Sunday night’s initial exit polls. In a narrow outcome, the broad right-wing bloc secured 173 seats, while the four opposition parties spanning the centrist-to-left-wing space won 176. Hardly Emphatic Win Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, already briefly prime minister in 2021–22, will now again be tasked with forming a government. In fact, her party’s 28.1 percent score on Sunday was its worst result in decades (slightly less even than a past bad result in 2018), and with a loss of seven seats compared to 2022. The Sweden Democrats lost ground (17.6 percent, down 3 percent and eleven seats from the previous election), overtaken by the Moderates (19.9 percent, with two more seats than last time). Researcher Tobias Hübinette suggests that the Sweden Democrats lost some of their voters to the Moderates but others — particularly young men — turned to smaller parties further to their right. These groups did not make it into parliament, but they represent a phenomenon worth monitoring given their violence and aggressive racism, as noted by Duroyan Fertl regarding one such force, the Örebro Party. There was slight growth for the other two parties in the center-right bloc: the Christian Democrats (6.2 percent, three more seats than in 2022) and the Liberals (5.4 percent, three more seats). Many polls had predicted the Liberals would fall below the 4 percent threshold, as part of their electorate was uncomfortable with their collaboration with the far right. On the opposition side, the Social Democrats’ losses are offset by gains from their potential allies. The Left Party increased its number of Riksdag seats from 24 to 29 (on 8.2 percent of the vote), while the Center gained one seat, on 7.1 percent. The Greens also performed well, gaining four seats and securing 6.1 percent. So, Kristersson’s right-wing bloc has lost its majority, and the far right has been stopped. These are two pieces of excellent news, but the hard part comes now. The opposition’s election campaign — especially that of the Social Democrats — was very timid, with significant concessions to right-wing rhetoric on immigration and criminal justice policy. Even on social issues (revitalizing the welfare state), Sweden’s biggest party did not seem to show the necessary combativeness or consistency, and this also explains why some of its voters turned to the radical left. Not by chance, Leonidas Aretakis, editor of socialist magazine Flamman , expressed some skepticism about whether defeat for the right-wing coalition would actually lead to the abandonment of right-wing policies. This skepticism is also driven by the balance of power among the opposition parties and, in particular, by the conflicting agendas of the radical left and the Center. The latter have made no secret of their preference for grand coalitions over cabinet cooperation with the Left Party. This latter has, however, made clear that it intends to join the government, believing that this offers it greater influence than providing external support to the Social Democrats (tactical approaches already used in the past and common in some Nordic countries). The opposition has major contradictions. The Center Party, champions of pro-market policies, had in fact long been partners of the traditional center right, only to distance themselves when these other forces moved closer to the Sweden Democrats. Conversely, the Left Party is calling for higher taxes on the wealthy, public investment, and the strengthening and decommodification of the welfare state. In particular, it is calling for universal dental care, as achieved by the Left’s Danish counterparts , and the removal of the profit motive from the education system — a highly sensitive issue in Sweden. Labor Relations This conflict is not limited to the world of party politics, for it also tells us something about what has become of Sweden and its model of work and welfare in recent decades. If in the 1970s economist Rudolf Meidner proposed moving beyond the welfare state and intervening directly in property relations via employee-owned funds, such proposals are now long in the past. Indeed, neoliberalism has taken its toll even on what was once the flagship of European social democracy. Today’s Stockholm is teeming with tech oligarchs: we need only think of the emblematic example of Spotify. During the lead-up to this election, industrialists, also given a platform in the Financial Times , publicly spoke out against the broad-left opposition’s proposals to increase taxation. Here as around Scandinavia, direct political pressure from the dominant economic actors is on the rise, as also recently seen in Denmark with businesses such as Maersk intervening in a similar debate on tax justice. This is a striking sign of renewed inequalities and a conflict between democracy and oligarchy that will also weigh on talks about Sweden’s next government. To properly analyze the outcome of Sunday’s election, we also ought to grasp the link between what happens in the corridors of power and what is going on in wider Swedish society. If Sweden was long the country that best embodied the social democratic compromise, this was based on a strong institutionalization of industrial relations. To understand whether a left-wing policy can be revived, this is perhaps where we need to start from. Recently, Tesla struck a blow to such an idea as it defeated a long strike by the engineering union demanding collective bargaining. Such a defeat demands further contemplation. For today, Sweden is increasingly marked by a deregulated and informal sector in the service industries, reliant on migrant workers, those with a migrant background, and workers from ethnic minorities. Some industrial disputes are taking place in the catering sector, with grassroots trade unionism uniting the struggle for better working conditions with the challenge to restrictive immigration policies and racism. This offers an important lesson in terms of rebuilding the prospects of an egalitarian society. Nor should we forget that, in this vote, new Swedish citizens of non-European origin were decisive in keeping the Sweden Democrats from power. This time, they abstained less and voted slightly more for the radical left and slightly less for the Social Democrats than they had previously. Palestine may, too, have played a role in their choice. In any case, Sunday’s election was another sign of how a better future will also depend on the active role of these parts of the working class.

articles.title: Report: The Working-Class Vote Is Not Lost
articles.author: Editors
articles.content: A new survey experiment from the Center for Working-Class Politics and Joan C. Williams finds that a six-part formula can lift Democrats’ working-class vote share by nearly 11 points. It also adds nearly 8 points among the party’s affluent, college-educated base. More than 40,000 respondents evaluated nearly 800,000 hypothetical candidate profiles, making the study one of the largest of its kind. The project was supported by Jacobin and the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung. The formula boils down to two imperatives: lead with working-class economics and connect with working-class values. Earlier this summer, Jared Abbott of the Center for Working-Class Politics (CWCP) and Joan C. Williams of the Equality Action Center (EAC) released “ The Left’s Coalition Crisis ,” a study of working-class and college-educated voters that showed how Democrats could hone their policy messaging to win back working-class voters without losing their college-educated base. Their second study, produced by Jacobin and fielded between April and June 2026, moves beyond testing messages in isolation and puts voters in a virtual voting booth. Respondents worked through a series of head-to-head matchups and chose which candidate they would vote for, or neither. Because every trait — demographics, class background, rhetoric, issue priorities, and economic and cultural positions — was assigned at random, the researchers can isolate how much each one moves the vote. The design also does something surveys rarely do: every matchup pits a complete Democratic candidate against a complete Republican one. Since party identification decides the large majority of votes, building partisanship into the experiment makes the estimates far more realistic, and more conservative, than those of most studies of this kind. The result is the Working-Class Win-O-Meter: a data-driven road map for winning back working-class voters, accompanied by a candidate tool kit and an online tool to allow people to better dig into our results. Some of Our Key Takeaways The formula moves the most votes among the voters progressives most need. Turning all six dials adds 10.9 points among working-class voters overall, but the gains are considerably bigger among the groups the party has struggled with: close to 14 points among working-class independents, about 13 points among 2024 nonvoters, and nearly 11 points among 2024 Donald Trump voters. At the district level that works out to a swing of 2 to 3 points in the two-party vote — more than Democrats’ 2024 losing margins in Wisconsin (0.9 points), Michigan (1.4), and Pennsylvania (1.7). Lead with working-class economics. Making working-class economics the campaign’s top priority, rather than defending democracy or leading with climate or culture-war issues, raises working-class support by 2.8 points. The payoff is largest with the swing voters the party needs back — 4 points among working-class independents and 3.3 among working-class 2024 Trump voters — and it also adds 2.3 points among the college-educated base. An earlier CWCP–EAC study found that ten of the twelve top working-class priorities are economic. One caution: whereas the college-educated base is fixated on prices, working-class voters (like black college graduates) care just as much about higher wages and economic opportunity. Progressives can (mostly) go bold on economics without paying a price. Where the study tested an ambitious version of an economic policy against a cautious one, on jobs, wages, unions, skills training, and industrial policy, the ambitious version matched or beat the cautious one. A $17 minimum wage, the highest tested, was also the most popular, outperforming $15 by 2 points and $12 by 3 points. Funding 500,000 skilled-trades apprenticeships a year performed as well as a modest employer tax break; a million public jobs rebuilding roads, bridges, and public buildings tied with simply funding job training; and $150 billion a year in manufacturing and infrastructure investment tied with a small tax credit. What working-class voters decline to reward are new tax-and-transfer programs with no connection to work, abstract market rules such as antitrust, and higher business tax rates. Form, not ambition, is what determines how a policy lands. The most popular policies defend what people already rely on and reward hard work. Of the forty-five Democratic economic policies tested, the most popular is one that has rarely topped the party’s affordability agenda: tuition-free community college. Protecting existing programs — the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), current student aid, Social Security benefits — generally outpolls sweeping new ones such as free four-year college. Among new programs, working-class voters favor those that make hard work pay off in good jobs, including apprenticeship programs and a guaranteed right to organize. This tracks a long-documented pattern: Americans are wary of redistribution in the abstract, until a program passes and becomes untouchable. Each policy is compared to the average across all economic positions tested (46.6%). The Type category indicates the more progressive or more moderate version of each issue. Read the table as a ranking of the strongest-testing policies relative to the average — affordability, defending existing popular programs, and worker power — rather than as a decisive margin for any one economic policy. It’s not only the economy: connecting with working-class values is worth up to 8 more points. The second headline cuts against James Carville’s old maxim. The study identifies five ways to do it, described in the takeaways that follow. Adopt culture and climate positions that resonate with working-class values. This is the most powerful of the five, adding 2.9 points overall and 3.3 among working-class Republicans. A validated scale identifies the values in question: loyalty to community and country, pride in hard work, respect for traditional institutions and for playing by the rules, personal security, and anti-elitism. Resonance does not mean surrendering the causes the college-educated base cares about; it means tying those causes to working-class values. “Abolish ICE,” as described below, is not popular in the abstract, yet 70 percent of working-class respondents back a path to citizenship for immigrants who have held jobs, paid taxes, and “stayed out of trouble.” “Moving to the center” carries no consistent advantage. Consistent with recent work by David Broockman and Joshua Kalla, the study finds no reliable payoff from moderating across the board. What costs votes is not progressive policy in general but a handful of positions like defunding the police and banning assault rifles. Reducing or redirecting police funding runs 5.7 points behind pairing body cameras with de-escalation training; banning assault rifles costs 4 points relative to universal background checks; and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement costs 2 points relative to reforming it. Progressive social positions framed in working-class values, by contrast, perform about as well as moderate ones. Leading on economics also marginally softens the penalty for progressive social stances — the “Mamdani effect” — trimming it from about 2.9 points to about 1.7. Pair those positions with an explicit statement of working-class values. Combining a resonant culture or climate policy with a direct appeal to working-class values adds another 1.6 points, and nearly 5 points among 2024 Trump voters. A candidate might, for instance, invoke loyalty to community and country by saying the country should look after its own communities first. Pairing a resonant policy with a working-class-values message adds +1.6 pp beyond the sum of the parts. Say you will listen to working-class people. Candidates who promise to listen more to working-class people, or to people from all walks of life, gain about 1.9 points, and a full 4 points among 2024 nonvoters. That beats centering the middle class, which is what Kamala Harris did in 2024 and what many other Democrats have done for decades. Use populist rhetoric and choose the right villain. Populist rhetoric adds 1.7 points, and most Democrats already use some version of it. The trap is the reflex to lean on expertise: candidates should praise the common sense of ordinary people rather than demand deference to experts. The target matters too. Attacking economic elites appears to lift support among the base, though only marginally significantly, and does little with working-class voters, whereas attacking political elites reaches a different group Democrats need, lifting support among middle- and upper-class moderates by 3.7 points. These results are for working-class respondents only. Across the full electorate, however, a people-first message that also names a political elite modestly outperforms a plain people-first message (+0.6 points); the almost negligible difference shown here is specific to the working class. Candidate class background matters. An elite professional résumé is the background working-class voters penalize most, and any non-elite background helps. But the blue-collar archetype is not required. Small business owners, pink-collar workers such as nurses and teachers, and service workers such as servers and retail clerks do just as well with working-class voters as blue-collar candidates. The dividing line is between elite professionals and everyone else, not between one kind of non-elite background and another. For the many Democrats who do come from elite backgrounds, this dial is worth about 1 point — a gap the other five can more than close. Candidates’ race and gender don’t matter to most working-class voters. The study independently randomized each candidate’s race (white, black, Latino, Asian) and gender. Neither had a significant effect on its own. The one exception is co-ethnic affinity: a black Democrat gains 3.3 points among black voters and a Latino Democrat gains 2.2 points among Hispanic voters, while white voters impose no penalty on a candidate of another race. There is no trade-off with the college-educated base. None of the six dials provokes a significant backlash among higher-income, college-educated Democrats, and the formula as a whole raises their support by about 7.8 points. Dial contributions are rounded to one decimal place. The Harris Test Case The formula’s gains are measured against a Harris 2024–style Democrat, and the comparison is not a straw man: every element of that profile scored poorly in the experiment. Harris foregrounded abortion rights and the threat to democracy over a wages-and-prices message. She struck a technocratic “opportunity economy” tone, leaning on expertise and credentials rather than the populist tone that scored far higher. She led with her professional résumé — prosecutor, attorney general, senator, vice president — the background working-class voters penalize most. And she repeatedly appealed to “the middle class” rather than “the working class,” a choice that ran about 2 points behind. As the authors put it, the Harris-style profile is assembled from the lower-scoring option on every dial. In the end the Win-O-Meter confirms what any skilled politician understands: voters back candidates who seem like them and who seem to like them. The prescription is simple — lead with working-class economics and connect with working-class values — and it points toward a big-tent coalition that does not require demonizing anyone. Read the full report here . Contact: Authors: jared@workingclasspolitics.org Press: publicity@workingclasspolitics.org

articles.title: UNITE HERE 26 and Teamsters 25 Hotel Workers On Simultaneous Strike At Encore Boston Harbor
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: On strike at Encore Boston Harbor (Working Mass) By: Vanessa Bartlett EVERETT – Workers at the Encore Boston Harbor, organized in bargaining units affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters Local 25 and UNITE HERE Local 26, went on strike September 4 in advance of Labor Day following the expiration of their contract on August 31. These 1350 hospitality workers have made the hotel-casino located at the juncture between Everett and Boston run since 2019, when Wynn Resorts opened the hotel on one of the three territories designated by the 2011 Expanded Gaming Act as legal gaming sites. While profits have risen, workers report that neither wages nor healthcare has kept up with company profits. Picketers marched back and forth in front of the main entrance and exit to the casino, on Broadway Street (Working Mass) On the Picket Line The picket line stretches along Broadway Street in Everett. A wide array of casino workers are hitting the streets every single day: housekeepers, cooks, servers, bartenders, slot attendants, warehouse workers, and drivers held signs, banged drums, and cheered at cars as they passed by honking in support. Chant leaders yelled into megaphones: “All day, all night – Encore workers on strike!” Encore workers created a boisterous drum line, donning ponchos to stay dry during rainy spells (Working Mass) According to UNITE HERE Local 26, 1,350 workers at the casino are on strike after 95% of union membership voted yes to the action on August 20. They are demanding pay that reflects the “five star” experience workers are expected to provide for casino guests, as well as maintaining healthcare benefits and job security. The unions are asking the public to “stay out!” of the resort while the strike is ongoing. Marina Guzman, a cage cashier at Encore, said that she found Encore’s response to workers’ demands “disheartening.” No word from them, no word at all to acknowledge the work that we do and all of the work that we put into the company every single day. Because I know that right now they’re having a hard time running the show without us. Marina Guzman, a cage cashier at Encore, called the casino’s lack of response “disheartening.” (Working Mass) “Coming in, I didn’t know of all the responsibilities that we would [have] as a cage cashier. I honestly thought I was just changing chips for people, but there’s so much we do in the back of house that nobody sees, that literally moves the whole casino,” said Guzman. Guzman and other cage cashiers were on the picket line because, according to Guzman, their pay and benefits are not in line with the compensation other workers at the casino receive. “We have a lot of catching up to do. And the fact that I see all of my cage coworkers here just lets me know that they’re fighting for the same things that I am, just as hard,” Guzman said. While she has only worked at Encore for three months, Guzman said she hopes to work at the casino for years to come. The Fall of Tipping Restaurant servers and bartenders are also demanding higher pay. Two cocktail servers explained that “tipping culture” has changed significantly, leading to lower than expected hourly wages for many servers at the casino. Iris Beltran, who has worked at Encore for four years, reported to Working Mass: The casino expects us to make, give or take, $400. We usually make about $200, maybe $300 [per shift]. Because of the thing with tipping culture, how people are like, ‘oh, you make enough because you’re getting tips,’… it’s heavily affecting us for sure. Maria Zubieta, another cocktail server, said she’s hopeful the contract will include a stipend for shoes. I got in trouble the other day because my shoes were too run-down. They’re like, ‘it’s not five stars’, you need new shoes. They’re not paying for those shoes. Servers are asking for a $2 raise. While it won’t close the gap between expected and actual wages for servers, Zubieta said that, “it’ll at least help a little, you know. A little more security, and with our health insurance, it will help with that kind of stuff, and that will take a big load off.” Currently, servers make $15 per hour: the Massachusetts state minimum wage. Beltran said: Guests expect top notch service, but we don’t get anything in return. So that’s what we’re trying to say… the money needs to come from somewhere, so if we’re trying to not expect tips from the guests, the casino should be the one [giving us] a raise. Teamsters 25 and UNITE HERE 26 press releases have pointed out the vast gap between Encore profits and worker compensation. Wynn Resorts reported a total operations revenue of $1.86 billion for just the second quarter of 2026 alone. According to Wynn Resorts, Encore Boston Harbor alone made $209.3 million in revenue for that quarter. Encore workers pose proudly for a photo. Workers said they feel their union is responsive and active. (Working Mass) Luke Williams, a flight attendant for American Airlines and union president of Association of Professional Flight Attendants (APFA)’s base in Boston (APFA BOS), was at the picket line on day one of the strike. “Local 26 is one of the biggest unions in the city, and flight attendants spend a lot of time in hotels, so we like to show our support for them whenever they go on strike,” Williams said. Williams – who joined DSA in December 2025 – has worked tirelessly on the picket line with other members providing Encore workers with strike support, including logistical support and helping workers file for unemployment. Williams explained further: DSA has gotten at least 38 people to sign up for shifts at the strike support office, which has mostly been helping workers file unemployment claims. Most people who volunteer will go to the picket lines as well, before and after their shifts. “The vibe on the picket line has been very upbeat, lots of people out there, it’s the first week of being out, so now things are starting to get more intense,” said Williams. “It seems to mean a lot when people show up for them when they haven’t seen people do that for them before.” One of the most important shows of solidarity that workers need is commitment to not cross the picket line and strike benefit fund contributions. Vanessa Bartlett is a member of Boston DSA and contributor to Working Mass. CORRECTION: Claims without concrete citation have been trimmed from a previous version of this article. The post UNITE HERE 26 and Teamsters 25 Hotel Workers On Simultaneous Strike At Encore Boston Harbor appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: In Defense of Abolition
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: At the July DSA National Political Committee (NPC) meeting, I proposed adding abolition to the Workers Deserve More program because I believe that abolishing capitalist policing and prisons is a fundamental demand of the socialist movement. I crafted the language carefully to clarify that we mean abolishing policing and prisons as institutions of capitalist rule, not conflating the abolition of capitalist policing and prisons with the abolition of every future social capacity for accountability and safety. The specific language we added is in italics: “Demilitarize police departments, disempower police unions, and redirect police and prison funding to public services, as steps towards abolishing the carceral forces of the capitalist state. ” This phrasing was eventually simplified to “towards abolishing the police and prison system.” This amendment was opposed by the Socialist Majority and Groundwork caucuses. Soon after the program’s launch, the abolition plank came under criticism from some DSA members , and several endorsed electeds explicitly disavowed the demand. Here, I argue that these reactions are rooted in a misunderstanding of the socialist tradition of abolition, a misreading of the lessons of 2020, and ultimately serve a reformist, anti-revolutionary conclusion. Abolition and Marxism Underlying the current debate over abolition are two recurring misunderstandings. The first, common among liberals and reformists, conflates the abolition of capitalist policing and prisons with the abolition of any future capacity for collective safety, accountability, or restraint. The second, more common in anarchist traditions, rejects the Marxist understanding of the state itself. Marxists reject both errors by analyzing policing and prisons as institutions historically produced by particular class relations, rather than timeless expressions of coercion. Resolving both misunderstandings requires a historical materialist theory of the state and its carceral institutions. A Marxist analysis asks the questions: What social relations produced this institution? What class function does it perform? What material conditions make it necessary? The Liberal Reformist Error Marxism differs from liberalism on the question of the state. Liberalism views the state as an essentially neutral instrument that can be put to different purposes. Marxism instead asks what class relations produced particular state institutions, what functions they serve within those relations, and how they can be transformed and how society’s material conditions can be changed. If, after the revolution, we have socialized the means of production, broken the profoundly corrupting ideological and cultural grip of capitalism, reimagined healthcare, housing, education, social services, and our communities around human need, what will we do with the rare person who remains hellbent on committing violence? How can we provide them with as much care and as many resources as we can while ensuring they are separated from the people they intend to hurt? It is absurd for a Marxist to equate revolutionary institutions of safety, accountability, and care with the institution of policing and prisons under capitalism or to abandon abolition as a rallying call. The possibilities of harm under any social arrangement do not establish the necessity of the institutions through which capitalist society currently manages that arrangement. Our task is to abolish those institutions and transform the social conditions that reproduce violence, not promise that socialism will make every violent act impossible. A related argument for “carceral minimalism” by Loïc Wacquant and, more recently, Paul Heideman in Jacobin , posits that abolition is not a viable path to social justice. Wacquant explicitly understands abolition to entail eliminating the “triad” of police, courts, and prisons rather than merely shrinking or reforming them. He correctly argues that we must take victims’ safety seriously and fight to materially reduce incarceration and state violence under existing conditions, but his framework never escapes a liberal capitalist horizon. He asks how policing, courts, and prisons can be made more limited and humane under capitalism, not whether the social relations that produce and sustain these institutions can be overcome. Indeed, his piece doesn’t mention socialism or communism a single time. The persistence of violence therefore becomes a reason to preserve some version of the institutions through which capitalist society currently manages it. A Marxist abolition rejects this inference and seeks to transform the material conditions that reproduce violence while developing new, democratically controlled capacities for collective safety, accountability, and repair. A socialist society might, where absolutely necessary, separate people who are a danger to others while providing them with care. But Wacquant’s insistence that a penal state, as a specialized apparatus of class domination, is a permanent requirement of complex society mistakes a historically specific institution of class rule for a universal social necessity. His “carceral minimalism” ultimately offers a program for managing coercion from within liberal capitalism, not a socialist alternative to it. The Anarchist Error The liberal error conflates abolition of policing with the abolition of all social accountability; the anarchist error mistakes the Marxist theory of the state for a defense of the capitalist state itself and locates the root of oppression primarily in hierarchy, bureaucracy, and coercion rather than the class relations that give the state and its instruments their political character. Lenin outlines his conception of the state in The State and Revolution . He writes that “the state is a product and a manifestation of the irreconcilability of class antagonisms.” It arises when society becomes divided into antagonistic classes. Here, Lenin quotes Engels, who writes that the state “becomes a power seemingly standing above society,” a “special, public power” that “does not directly coincide” with the people, consisting of “special bodies of armed men,” and “a standing army and police ” as “the chief instruments of state power.” Lenin does not define the state or policing merely as a form of coercion but as the product and a manifestation of the irreconcilability of class antagonisms. The capitalist state is an organ of capitalist rule produced by class society and used by the capitalist class to maintain its domination. The police serve as one of its chief instruments. The proletarian state exists to defend the revolution against capitalist counterrevolution while creating the material conditions for its own obsolescence. As class antagonisms are overcome, coercive institutions produced by class antagonisms lose their social basis. Some critics of abolition correctly identify this need to defend the revolution, but both fail to understand the difference in political character of coercion under socialism and fail to envision a world beyond class antagonism. This is ultimately an anti-communist perspective. Marx’s analysis of the Paris Commune in The Civil War in France makes this distinction concrete. He argues “the working class cannot simply lay hold of the ready-made state machinery, and wield it for its own purposes,” specifically identifying the standing army, police, and bureaucracy. Marx praises the commune because it “got rid” of these institutions and transferred their functions to serve the working class, rather than simply inheriting them: “Instead of continuing to be the agent of the Central Government, the police was at once stripped of its political attributes, and turned into the responsible, and at all times revocable, agent of the Commune … having once got rid of the standing army and the police —the physical force elements of the old government.” He continues: “Wonderful, indeed, was the change the Commune had wrought in Paris! No more corpses at the morgue, no nocturnal burglaries, scarcely any robberies; in fact, for the first time since the days of February 1848, the streets of Paris were safe, and that without any police of any kind.” This is the materialist basis for a socialist abolitionism. We seek the abolition of prisons and policing as institutions of capitalist domination, while recognizing that socialism will have to solve real problems that capitalism currently purports to address through those institutions. The Marxist question is not whether those problems exist nor whether society may ever require coercive measures, but what social relations make particular forms of coercion necessary, who controls them, what class interests they serve, and how the institutions reproduce the conditions that make them necessary. In this way, abolition is not a demand to abolish social protection or accountability but a demand to abolish the capitalist form through which these problems are organized, and to transform the underlying social conditions so that institutions of class domination are unnecessary. The Rise of Abolition Tracing the roots of abolition reveals its significance to the socialist movement. During the George Floyd uprisings in 2020, abolition was a central concern in socialist politics. At its strongest, the movement came to understand abolition as not only a moral appeal against punishment in the abstract but a fight against police and prisons as institutions rooted in the history of slavery, racial capitalism, and class rule, whose abolition required transforming the social conditions that reproduce them. This framing is rooted in the Black radical socialist tradition. From W.E.B. Du Bois to Angela Davis and Ruth Wilson Gilmore, abolition has long meant abolition of the social order that makes systems of policing and prisons necessary while constructing new capacities for collective life. Du Bois located the origins of modern policing and imprisonment in the unfinished project of abolishing slavery. As he wrote in Black Reconstruction , “The slave went free; stood a brief moment in the sun; then moved back again toward slavery.” The overthrow of chattel slavery was followed by new forms of racial domination, including convict leasing, Jim Crow, debt peonage, and modern policing, extending slavery’s social function under capitalism by ensuring a disciplined and racially stratified labor force produced by Black oppression. Gilmore extends this analysis to the political economy of prisons in the neoliberal era. The disruption and disorganization of the working class is essential to the functioning of the system. As she writes in Abolition Geography, “Put simply, capitalism requires inequality and racism enshrines it. Thus criminalization and mass incarceration are class war.” In Golden Gulag , Gilmore analyzes how the carceral system became a means of managing the crises produced by neoliberal capitalism . The economic crises arising from the neoliberal transformation of the capitalist economy produced a massive increase in surplus labor — a growing population of people whose labor was considered superfluous to capital’s needs. Because of the racialized hierarchy of social relations in the United States, one key response was a massively intensified campaign to criminalize Black and Latino populations, and a concomitant enormous growth of the carceral state. This transformed a surplus population into one to be managed and contained, which weakened the possibility of the solidarity required to meaningfully challenge capitalism. As Gilmore explains, “Capital must be able to get rid of workers whose labor power is no longer desirable — whether permanently, by mechanical or human replacement, or temporarily by layoffs — and have access to new or previously idled labor as the need arises. These necessities, as Marx’s science of capital accumulation demonstrates, are not due to the personalities or preferences of heads of firms: CEOs who resist such “adjustments” to the labor force jeopardize profits.” Today we see the hyper-criminalization of immigrants as serving a similarly useful role for capitalism. U.S. imperialism creates the conditions for mass migration through practices of unequal exchange that impoverish the Global South, where the resulting sub-subsistence level wages force workers to migrate for survival. The creation of a maximally exploitable immigrant labor produces an underclass of laborers whose vulnerability is targeted to drive down the power of the working class as a whole. (See Migration As Economic Imperialism by Immanuel Ness.) Declining opportunities for profitable investment for capital dictate that workers in the United States must be disciplined to accept less, and a terrified, hyper-exploitable working class continues to lower the floor for the working class as a whole. As Mark Neocleous summarizes in A Critical Theory of Police Power, “Capital is nothing less than a social war and the conflict between classes the most significant civil war in history. Yet this class war is carried out as a generalized police war.” Given the centrality of policing and prisons to capitalist accumulation within the imperial core, abandoning abolition would mean abandoning class war. Abolition’s Retreat Today there is a growing retreat from the Marxist and Black radical frameworks. Much of the current debate frames abolition as an abstract hypothetical about whether any society will ever require coercion or restraint. This framing detaches itself from the concrete institutions and social relations through which policing is organized under capitalism. Instead of asking what police and prisons are as institutions that manage the contradictions of racial capitalism, it asks whether a generalized form of public safety might exist in an imagined future society. In contrast, a Marxist approach asks us to begin not with abstractions but with the concrete institutions and social relations that produce institutions. Police and prisons are not neutral responses to human conflict but historically specific institutions expanded alongside capitalism, colonialism, and racial domination. The consequences of this mistake are significant. Once abolition is framed as an abstract proposition that all coercion must vanish forever, it becomes easy to dismiss as unrealistic. Instead of being seen as a strategy for dismantling institutions that reproduce capitalism and racial domination, it’s framed as either the fantastical idealism of anarchism or the limited purview of policy reform. It’s important to acknowledge that this retreat from abolition emerges from a real contradiction facing the socialist movement. The George Floyd uprising was the largest mass rebellion against policing in a generation, yet it produced few lasting structural victories. It’s reasonable to ask whether the movement’s politics, including the rallying cry to abolish the police, contributed to that outcome. But this mistakes the primary lessons of 2020. The principal failure was not that abolition proved to be bad politics or messaging, but that the socialist movement lacked the durable organization, institutions, mass base, and independent politics necessary to adequately absorb the energy of the uprising and carry it forward once the streets emptied. This retreat also cannot be understood apart from the intensity of the capitalist and political backlash against the politics of 2020. As Alex Karakatsanis has shown , the liberal establishment and corporate media worked overtime to co-opt the outrage into reforms that left the core institutions intact and quickly began a massive propaganda campaign aimed at selling the lie that crime was spiraling out of control. Progressive politicians and liberal media were eager to return to business as usual, abandoning the rhetoric of 2020 as quickly as they could and once again supporting ballooning police budgets, happy to paper over their inability to meet people’s needs by throwing money at the criminalization of poverty in service of capital. At the same time, much of the left increasingly reduced policing to a question of municipal budgets rather than understanding it as a central institution of capitalist political power. The basis of this liberal retreat from abolition is clear. The question remaining is: What are the core contradictions driving the left’s retreat? Electoralism and Reformism DSA’s electoral successes have been expanding at a rapid rate. As a result, anything that appears to threaten this success naturally faces special scrutiny. This reformist logic was recently articulated by Mayor Mamdani , who, when asked about his breaks with DSA, stated: “Especially when it comes to public safety, I’ve been very clear that we have our police force, we have prisons, we have jails. The purpose of these is also to ensure we are delivering safety & justice.” Indeed, members of the Socialist Majority Caucus and Groundwork caucuses, the Jacobin editorial board, and a number of DSA electeds and aligned candidates have argued that abolition should be de-emphasized or abandoned because it is electorally unpopular or idealistic. Often, this takes the form of stressing the urgency of passing a candidate’s affordability agenda at all costs. This risks pushing DSA towards the pitfalls of tailism and economism , subverting our political program in favor of what is immediately achievable rather than using our political organization to expand what workers see as possible. It is of course necessary to adapt the way we communicate depending on the context. Every mass movement must distinguish between propaganda, agitation, and the demands most appropriate to a particular audience. The error lies in retreating from a political plank altogether to avoid the strategic challenge in the first place. Whether a particular candidate campaigns on abolition, and to what extent, is a tactical question. But allowing that question to redefine the political program of a socialist movement reverses the proper relationship between the movement and its elected officials. Independent socialist organizations must expand the political horizon of the working class, not narrow it according to what elected officials can comfortably defend. DSA’s success is because of our steadfast adherence to our core principles, not in spite of it. Our organization has grown significantly since our program was released. When another moment like 2020 occurs (and it is inevitable), the working class will remember where we stood. Part of this challenge reflects the need for DSA to develop further towards a party of the working class: an organization with all the structure, resources, political coherence, and discipline to support our candidates in standing firm rather than leaving them isolated in their respective political arenas to fend off attacks and feel compelled to distance themselves from or abandon demands in order to win reelection or fulfill campaign promises. That requires a commitment to fulfilling our Convention mandate to build DSA’s capacity to act as an independent political organization: strengthening the National Electoral Commission’s ability to coordinate our electoral work nationally while building robust Socialists in Office programs at the local level, so our electeds remain closely connected to DSA and are not left to navigate the pressures of office alone. It also requires building connective tissue and infrastructure across chapters and between national and local levels so that DSA can act as a unified political organization rather than a collection of isolated electoral campaigns. Of course, embracing an abolitionist horizon does not mean DSA and our electeds should abstain from reform. Socialists in office should pursue every reform that weakens the carceral state, defunds police, reduces incarceration, and expands healthcare, but they should do so as part of a strategy aimed at the eventual abolition of policing and prisons rather than as an end in itself. For Marxists, abolition is not an abstract moral principle or a distant utopia. It’s the unfinished struggle to complete the destruction of slavery’s institutional legacy and embrace Marx’s call to seize the machinery of the state, smash it altogether, and usher in a new social order. We should recall Eugene Debs’s exhortation: While there is a soul in prison, we are not free.
